claim: Termination of messenger RNA translation in Bacteria and Archaea is initiated by release factors (RFs) 1 or 2 recognizing a stop codon in the ribosomal A site.
source: Termination of messenger RNA translation in Bacteria and Archaea is initiated by release factors (RFs) 1 or 2 recognizing a stop codon in the ribosomal A site and releasing the peptide from the P-site transfer RNA.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by citations in the introduction section (Kisselev and Buckingham, 2000; Klaholz, 2011).

claim: RF1 recognizes UAA and UAG stop codons.
source: RF1 and RF2 induce release of the polypeptide attached to the P-site transfer RNA (tRNA) (for reviews, see Kisselev and Buckingham, 2000; Klaholz, 2011).
evidence: Stated in the introduction with citation support (Kisselev and Buckingham, 2000; Klaholz, 2011).

claim: RF2 recognizes UAA and UGA stop codons.
source: class-1 release factor 1 (RF1), recognizing UAA and UAG, or 2 (RF2), recognizing UAA and UGA.
evidence: Explicitly stated in the introduction.

claim: RF1 and RF2 induce release of the polypeptide attached to the P-site tRNA.
source: RF1 and RF2 induce release of the polypeptide attached to the P-site transfer RNA (tRNA) (for reviews, see Kisselev and Buckingham, 2000; Klaholz, 2011).
evidence: Stated with citation support.

claim: Release of class-1 RF from the post-polypeptide release complex is facilitated by RF3 in a GTP-dependent manner.
source: Subsequent release of the class-1 RF from the post-polypeptide release complex (RC) is facilitated by a class-2 release factor, the G-protein RF3, in a GTP-dependent manner (Freistroffer et al., 1997).
evidence: Stated with citation support (Freistroffer et al., 1997).

claim: RF3 is a G-protein.
source: a class-2 release factor, the G-protein RF3
evidence: Explicitly stated in the text.

claim: RF3, IF2, EF-Tu, and EF-G constitute a set of four major translational GTPases.
source: RF3, along with initiation factor 2 (IF2), elongation factor Tu (EF-Tu) and elongation factor G (EF-G), constitute a set of four major translational GTPases (Zavialov and Ehrenberg, 2003).
evidence: Stated with citation support (Zavialov and Ehrenberg, 2003).

claim: Free RF3 has high affinity to GDP.
source: Free RF3 has high affinity to GDP; the RF3•GDP complex dissociates very slowly into RF3 and GDP and, thus, free RF3 in the cytoplasm exists mainly in the GDP-form (Zavialov et al., 2001, 2002).
evidence: Stated with citation support (Zavialov et al., 2001, 2002).

claim: The RF3•GDP complex dissociates very slowly into RF3 and GDP.
source: Free RF3 has high affinity to GDP; the RF3•GDP complex dissociates very slowly into RF3 and GDP and, thus, free RF3 in the cytoplasm exists mainly in the GDP-form (Zavialov et al., 2001, 2002).
evidence: Stated with citation support (Zavialov et al., 2001, 2002).

claim: Free RF3 in the cytoplasm exists mainly in the GDP-form.
source: Free RF3 has high affinity to GDP; the RF3•GDP complex dissociates very slowly into RF3 and GDP and, thus, free RF3 in the cytoplasm exists mainly in the GDP-form (Zavialov et al., 2001, 2002).
evidence: Stated with citation support (Zavialov et al., 2001, 2002).

claim: For EF-Tu, GDP exchange to GTP is conferred by the guanine nucleotide exchange factor EF-Ts off the ribosome.
source: In contrast to EF-Tu, for which GDP exchange to GTP is conferred by the guanine nucleotide exchange factor EF-Ts off the ribosome, the guanine nucleotide exchange factor for RF3 is the ribosome in complex with a class-1 RF (Zavialov et al., 2001).
evidence: Stated with citation support (Zavialov et al., 2001).

claim: The guanine nucleotide exchange factor for RF3 is the ribosome in complex with a class-1 RF.
source: In contrast to EF-Tu, for which GDP exchange to GTP is conferred by the guanine nucleotide exchange factor EF-Ts off the ribosome, the guanine nucleotide exchange factor for RF3 is the ribosome in complex with a class-1 RF (Zavialov et al., 2001).
evidence: Stated with citation support (Zavialov et al., 2001).

claim: GDP-to-GTP exchange occurs rapidly on free IF2 and EF-G in the absence of any exchange factor.
source: GDP-to-GTP exchange occurs rapidly on free IF2 and EF-G in the absence of any exchange factor.
evidence: Stated in the introduction.

claim: As RF3•GDP enters the class-1 RF-bound ribosome, GDP is readily exchanged for GTP, provided the peptide has been hydrolyzed off the P-site tRNA.
source: As RF3•GDP enters the class-1 RF-bound ribosome, GDP is readily exchanged for GTP, provided the peptide has been hydrolyzed off the P-site tRNA (Zavialov et al., 2002).
evidence: Stated with citation support (Zavialov et al., 2002).

claim: GTP binding to RF3 is accompanied by conformational changes in both RF3 and the ribosome.
source: GTP binding is accompanied by conformational changes in both RF3 and the ribosome (Gao et al., 2007).
evidence: Stated with citation support (Gao et al., 2007).

claim: The change in ribosome structure promotes rapid release of the class-1 RF followed by GTP hydrolysis.
source: The change in ribosome structure promotes rapid release of the class-1 RF followed by GTP hydrolysis and, finally, release of RF3 in the GDP form from the ribosome (Zavialov et al., 2001, 2002).
evidence: Stated with citation support (Zavialov et al., 2001, 2002).

claim: After GTP hydrolysis, RF3 is released in the GDP form from the ribosome.
source: The change in ribosome structure promotes rapid release of the class-1 RF followed by GTP hydrolysis and, finally, release of RF3 in the GDP form from the ribosome (Zavialov et al., 2001, 2002).
evidence: Stated with citation support (Zavialov et al., 2001, 2002).

claim: Cryo-EM structures of A-site bound class-1 RFs interacting with their cognate stop codons have been reported.
source: Structurally, termination of mRNA translation has been characterized by cryo-EM (Rawat et al., 2006) and X-ray crystal (Petry et al., 2005; Laurberg et al., 2008) structures of A-site bound class-1 RFs interacting with their cognate stop codons.
evidence: Stated with citation support (Rawat et al., 2006; Petry et al., 2005; Laurberg et al., 2008).

claim: X-ray crystal structures of A-site bound class-1 RFs interacting with their cognate stop codons have been reported.
source: Structurally, termination of mRNA translation has been characterized by cryo-EM (Rawat et al., 2006) and X-ray crystal (Petry et al., 2005; Laurberg et al., 2008) structures of A-site bound class-1 RFs interacting with their cognate stop codons.
evidence: Stated with citation support (Petry et al., 2005; Laurberg et al., 2008).

claim: Structures of class-1 RFs have contributed to understanding of the principles of stop codon recognition by class-1 RFs.
source: These structures have, in conjunction with molecular dynamics simulations (Sund et al., 2010), contributed to present-day understanding of the principles of stop codon recognition by class-1 RFs and of their activation of the peptidyl transfer center for hydrolysis of the ester bond in peptidyl-tRNA.
evidence: Stated with citation support (Sund et al., 2010).

claim: The X-ray crystal structure of free RF3•GDP has been reported.
source: In addition, the X-ray crystal structure of free RF3•GDP (Gao et al., 2007) and cryo-EM (Gao et al., 2007) and crystal (Jin et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2012) structures of post-termination and post class-1 RF release ribosomes in complex with RF3 bound to GTP-analogs are known.
evidence: Stated with citation support (Gao et al., 2007).

claim: Cryo-EM structures of post-termination ribosomes in complex with RF3 bound to GTP-analogs have been reported.
source: In addition, the X-ray crystal structure of free RF3•GDP (Gao et al., 2007) and cryo-EM (Gao et al., 2007) and crystal (Jin et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2012) structures of post-termination and post class-1 RF release ribosomes in complex with RF3 bound to GTP-analogs are known.
evidence: Stated with citation support (Gao et al., 2007; Jin et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2012).

claim: RF3•GDP(N/C)P-bound intersubunit-rotated ribosomes are incompatible with class-1 RF binding.
source: Furthermore, these structures of RF3•GDP(N/C)P-bound intersubunit-rotated ribosomes are incompatible with class-1 RF binding (Gao et al., 2007; Jin et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2012), as previously suggested from biochemical data (Zavialov and Ehrenberg, 2003).
evidence: Stated with citation support (Gao et al., 2007; Jin et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2012; Zavialov and Ehrenberg, 2003).

claim: The study presents cryo-EM density maps of the E. coli ribosomal post-peptide-release complex in association with RF1 alone.
source: In this study we present cryo-EM density maps of the E. coli ribosomal post-peptide-release complex (RC; 70S, tRNAfMet and [Met, stop]-mRNA) in association with RF1 alone and in association with both apo-RF3 and RF1.
evidence: Stated in the introduction as a primary finding of the study.

claim: The study presents cryo-EM density maps of the E. coli ribosomal post-peptide-release complex in association with both apo-RF3 and RF1.
source: In this study we present cryo-EM density maps of the E. coli ribosomal post-peptide-release complex (RC; 70S, tRNAfMet and [Met, stop]-mRNA) in association with RF1 alone and in association with both apo-RF3 and RF1.
evidence: Stated in the introduction as a primary finding of the study.

claim: Complexes were obtained at a residual concentration of free GDP and in the absence of GTP.
source: Complexes were obtained at a residual concentration of free GDP and in the absence of GTP.
evidence: Stated in the introduction describing experimental conditions.

claim: The RC-RF1•RF3 complex contains a novel form of RF1 in close interaction with the apo-form of RF3.
source: We show that the latter complex contains a novel form of RF1 in close interaction with the apo-form of RF3 and furthermore infer a direct interaction of RF3 with ribosomal protein L7/L12.
evidence: Stated in the introduction as a primary finding of the study.

claim: RF3 directly interacts with ribosomal protein L7/L12.
source: We show that the latter complex contains a novel form of RF1 in close interaction with the apo-form of RF3 and furthermore infer a direct interaction of RF3 with ribosomal protein L7/L12.
evidence: Stated in the introduction as a primary finding of the study.

claim: The conformation of RF3 in the RC-RF1•RF3 complex is distinct from those of free RF3•GDP and ribosome-bound RF3•GDP(C/N)P.
source: The conformation of RF3 is distinct from those of free RF3•GDP and ribosome-bound RF3•GDP(C/N)P.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a primary finding.

claim: The conformation of RF1 in the RC-RF1•RF3 complex differs from those observed in RF3-lacking ribosomal complexes.
source: Furthermore, the conformation of RF1 differs from those observed in RF3-lacking ribosomal complexes.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a primary finding.

claim: RF1 and RF3 were present together on the ribosome in close to 1:1 ratios with S1 in the absence of extra added GDP.
source: The gel showed RF1 and RF3 together on the ribosome in close to 1:1 ratios with S1 in the absence of extra added GDP (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: Stated in the results section and supported by gel analysis shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: When the concentration of extra GDP was increased, the RF3 band decreased gradually and virtually disappeared at 200 μM extra GDP concentration.
source: When the concentration of extra GDP was increased, the RF3 band decreased gradually and virtually disappeared at 200 μM extra GDP concentration, while the RF1 band remained at 1:1 stoichiometry with S1 (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: Stated in the results section and supported by gel analysis shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: The RF1 band remained at 1:1 stoichiometry with S1 when extra GDP concentration was increased.
source: When the concentration of extra GDP was increased, the RF3 band decreased gradually and virtually disappeared at 200 μM extra GDP concentration, while the RF1 band remained at 1:1 stoichiometry with S1 (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: Stated in the results section and supported by gel analysis shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: In the absence of RF1, no binding of RF3 to the ribosome was detected even with no extra added GDP.
source: In a second, similar, experiment performed in the absence of RF1, we detected no binding of RF3 to the ribosome—neither to RC nor to 70S—even with no extra added GDP (Figure 1C).
evidence: Stated in the results section and supported by gel analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Apo-RF3 formed a stable complex with the RF1-bound ribosome at low concentration of free GDP.
source: From these experiments we could infer that apo-RF3 formed a stable complex with the RF1-bound ribosome at low concentration of free GDP.
evidence: Stated in the results section as an inference from the gel data.

claim: In the absence of RF1 or at elevated GDP concentration, RF3 did not form a stable complex with the ribosome.
source: However, in the absence of RF1 or at elevated GDP concentration, RF3 did not form a stable complex with the ribosome, in line with previous conclusions based on less direct experimental evidence (Zavialov et al., 2001, 2002).
evidence: Stated in the results section with citation support (Zavialov et al., 2001, 2002).

claim: RF3•GDP does not form a stable complex with the RF1-bound ribosome.
source: Thus, RF3•GDP does not form a stable complex with the RF1-bound ribosome, and we therefore conclude that the reconstituted ribosomal release complex presented in lane 1 of the gel presented in Figure 1A contains the apo-form of RF3 along with RF1.
evidence: Stated in the results section as a conclusion from the gel data.

claim: The reconstituted ribosomal release complex contains the apo-form of RF3 along with RF1.
source: Thus, RF3•GDP does not form a stable complex with the RF1-bound ribosome, and we therefore conclude that the reconstituted ribosomal release complex presented in lane 1 of the gel presented in Figure 1A contains the apo-form of RF3 along with RF1.
evidence: Stated in the results section as a conclusion from the gel data.

claim: Three classes were identified in total from the cryo-EM image classification.
source: Three classes were identified in total.
evidence: Stated in the results section describing the reconstruction process.

claim: The first class (∼14,000 projection images) yielded a density map of the 70S ribosome in MS-I conformation carrying a P-site tRNA and fragments of an E-site tRNA but with no trace of RF1 or RF3.
source: The first class (∼14,000 projection images; Figure 2—figure supplement 2) yielded a density map of the 70S ribosome in MS-I conformation carrying a P-site tRNA and fragments of an E-site tRNA but with no trace of RF1 or RF3; this class will be disregarded in the following analysis.
evidence: Stated in the results section and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The second class (∼43,000 projection images) yielded a density map of the 70S ribosome in MS-I conformation carrying RF1 in the A site, a tRNA in the P site and trace density of a tRNA in the E site.
source: The second class (∼43,000 projection images; Figure 2A–C) yielded a density map of the 70S ribosome in MS-I conformation carrying RF1 in the A site, a tRNA in the P site and trace density of a tRNA in the E site
evidence: Stated in the results section and supported by Figure 2A–C.

claim: The third class (∼29,000 projection images) yielded a density map of the 70S ribosome in MS-I conformation carrying apo-RF3, RF1, a P-site tRNA and trace density of an E-site tRNA.
source: the third class (∼29,000 projection images; Figure 2D–F) yielded a density map of the 70S ribosome in MS-I conformation carrying apo-RF3, RF1, a P-site tRNA and trace density of an E-site tRNA.
evidence: Stated in the results section and supported by Figure 2D–F.

claim: RF1 and RF3 were identified by their shapes and positions on the ribosome.
source: RF1 and RF3 were identified by their shapes and positions on the ribosome (Rawat et al., 2006; Gao et al., 2007, respectively).
evidence: Stated in the results section with citation support (Rawat et al., 2006; Gao et al., 2007).

claim: In the RC-RF1 map, domain 3 of RF1 reaches into the peptidyl-transferase center of the 50S ribosomal subunit.
source: In the RC-RF1 map, domain 3 of RF1 reaches into the peptidyl-transferase center of the 50S ribosomal subunit and the super-domain 2/4 of RF1 occupies the decoding center of the 30S ribosomal subunit.
evidence: Stated in the results section describing the RC-RF1 map.

claim: In the RC-RF1 map, the super-domain 2/4 of RF1 occupies the decoding center of the 30S ribosomal subunit.
source: In the RC-RF1 map, domain 3 of RF1 reaches into the peptidyl-transferase center of the 50S ribosomal subunit and the super-domain 2/4 of RF1 occupies the decoding center of the 30S ribosomal subunit.
evidence: Stated in the results section describing the RC-RF1 map.

claim: In the RC-RF1 map, domain 1 of RF1 contacts the N-terminal domain of protein L11 (L11-NTD) and reaches toward the 30S subunit beak.
source: In addition, domain 1 of RF1 contacts the N-terminal domain of protein L11 (L11-NTD) and reaches toward the 30S subunit beak (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: Stated in the results section and supported by Figure 2A–C.

claim: In the RC-RF1•RF3 map, domain 3 of apo-RF3 contacts domain 1 of RF1 and extends toward the spur of the 30S subunit.
source: In the RC-RF1•RF3 map, domain 3 of apo-RF3 contacts domain 1 of RF1 and extends toward the spur of the 30S subunit (Figure 2D–F).
evidence: Stated in the results section and supported by Figure 2D–F.

claim: Domain 3 of apo-RF3 interacts with 30S protein S12.
source: Domain 3 of apo-RF3 interacts with 30S protein S12, as observed earlier for RF3 in complex with non-hydrolyzable GTP analogs—GDP(C/N)P—bound to the ribosome in the rotated MS-II form in the absence of a class-1 RF (Gao et al., 2007; Jin et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2012).
evidence: Stated in the results section with citation support (Gao et al., 2007; Jin et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2012).

claim: There is only a weak interaction between domain 2 of apo-RF3 and 16S rRNA helix 5.
source: However, we observe only a weak interaction between domain 2 of apo-RF3 and 16S rRNA helix 5, whereas the interaction of RF3•GDP(C/N)P with this helix is strong (Gao et al., 2007; Jin et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2012).
evidence: Stated in the results section with citation support (Gao et al., 2007; Jin et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2012).

claim: The interaction of RF3•GDP(C/N)P with 16S rRNA helix 5 is strong.
source: However, we observe only a weak interaction between domain 2 of apo-RF3 and 16S rRNA helix 5, whereas the interaction of RF3•GDP(C/N)P with this helix is strong (Gao et al., 2007; Jin et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2012).
evidence: Stated in the results section with citation support (Gao et al., 2007; Jin et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2012).

claim: Domain 1 of RF1 contacts both domain 3 of RF3 and L11-NTD in the RC-RF1•RF3 map.
source: Furthermore, we observe domain 1 of RF1 contacting both domain 3 of RF3 and L11-NTD (Figure 2D–F and Figure 2—figure supplement 3B, D).
evidence: Stated in the results section and supported by Figure 2D–F and Figure 2—figure supplement 3B, D.

claim: A large conformational change of RF1 occurs in response to the binding of apo-RF3.
source: Comparison of the RF1 conformation in our RC-RF1•RF3 map (Figure 2D–F and Figure 2—figure supplement 3B, D) with that in the RC-RF1 map (Figure 2A–C and Figure 2—figure supplement 3A, C) reveals a large conformational change of RF1 in response to the binding of apo-RF3 resulting in the formation of a bridge from apo-RF3 via RF1 to L11 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Stated in the results section and supported by Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The binding of apo-RF3 results in the formation of a bridge from apo-RF3 via RF1 to L11.
source: Comparison of the RF1 conformation in our RC-RF1•RF3 map (Figure 2D–F and Figure 2—figure supplement 3B, D) with that in the RC-RF1 map (Figure 2A–C and Figure 2—figure supplement 3A, C) reveals a large conformational change of RF1 in response to the binding of apo-RF3 resulting in the formation of a bridge from apo-RF3 via RF1 to L11 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Stated in the results section and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Domain 1 of apo-RF3 is in the vicinity of, but not in contact with, L6/SRL.
source: Domain 1 of apo-RF3 is in the vicinity of, but not in contact with, L6/SRL (Figure 2G,H, Figure 3A).
evidence: Stated in the results section and supported by Figure 2G,H and Figure 3A.

claim: A direct contact between RF3 and L6/SRL was observed in the post class-1 RF-release RC-RF3•GDP(C/N)P maps.
source: In contrast, a direct contact between RF3 and L6/SRL was observed in the post class-1 RF-release RC-RF3•GDP(C/N)P maps (Figure 3B) (Klaholz et al., 2004; Gao et al., 2007; Jin et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2012), with the ribosome in the rotated MS-II state.
evidence: Stated in the results section with citation support (Klaholz et al., 2004; Gao et al., 2007; Jin et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2012) and supported by Figure 3B.

claim: In the apo-RF3 and RF1-containing complex, apo-RF3 is docked to the RC framework only through domain 3.
source: Hence, in the apo-RF3 and RF1-containing complex, apo-RF3 is docked to the RC framework only through domain 3, while in the RC-RF3•GDP(C/N)P maps RF3•GDP(C/N)P is seen to be firmly docked to RC through contacts involving domains 1, 2 and 3 (Klaholz et al., 2004; Gao et al., 2007; Jin et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2012).
evidence: Stated in the results section with citation support (Klaholz et al., 2004; Gao et al., 2007; Jin et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2012).

claim: In the RC-RF3•GDP(C/N)P maps, RF3•GDP(C/N)P is firmly docked to RC through contacts involving domains 1, 2 and 3.
source: Hence, in the apo-RF3 and RF1-containing complex, apo-RF3 is docked to the RC framework only through domain 3, while in the RC-RF3•GDP(C/N)P maps RF3•GDP(C/N)P is seen to be firmly docked to RC through contacts involving domains 1, 2 and 3 (Klaholz et al., 2004; Gao et al., 2007; Jin et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2012).
evidence: Stated in the results section with citation support (Klaholz et al., 2004; Gao et al., 2007; Jin et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2012).

claim: Domain 1 of RF3 contains an 'arc-like' density clearly separated from the density of the NTD of L11.
source: Domain 1 of RF3 contains an 'arc-like' density (Figure 2G,H, Figure 2—figure supplement 3B, D) clearly separated from the density of the NTD of L11.
evidence: Stated in the results section and supported by Figure 2G,H and Figure 2—figure supplement 3B, D.

claim: An 'arc-like' density was observed in a similar position, but fully bridging RF3 to L11-NTD in the RC-RF3•GDPNP map.
source: An 'arc-like' density was observed in a similar position, but fully bridging RF3 to L11-NTD in the RC-RF3•GDPNP map (Figure 3B) (Gao et al., 2007).
evidence: Stated in the results section with citation support (Gao et al., 2007) and supported by Figure 3B.

claim: In the case of EF-G, the bridge was identified as the CTD of L7/L12.
source: In the case of EF-G, the bridge was subsequently identified as the CTD of L7/L12 (henceforth denoted L12; the difference being an N-terminal acetylation in case of L7) (Datta et al., 2005).
evidence: Stated in the results section with citation support (Datta et al., 2005).

claim: The interaction between L12-CTD and apo-RF3 without involvement of L11-NTD has not previously been reported.
source: The interaction we observe in the present RC-RF1•RF3 map between L12-CTD and apo-RF3 without involvement of L11-NTD has not previously been reported.
evidence: Stated in the results section as a novel finding.

claim: In the RC-RF1 map, helices α2 and α3 in domain 1 are observed in contact with the P-rich 310-helix in L11-NTD.
source: In our RC-RF1 map, helices α2 and α3 in domain 1 are observed in contact with the P-rich 310-helix in L11-NTD (Figure 4A,D) (Petry et al., 2005; Rawat et al., 2006; Laurberg et al., 2008).
evidence: Stated in the results section with citation support (Petry et al., 2005; Rawat et al., 2006; Laurberg et al., 2008) and supported by Figure 4A,D.

claim: In the RC-RF1•RF3 map, an RF1-mediated structural bridge is observed between L11-NTD and domain 3 of RF3.
source: In the RC-RF1•RF3 map, we observe an RF1-mediated structural bridge between L11-NTD and domain 3 of RF3 (Figure 4E).
evidence: Stated in the results section and supported by Figure 4E.

claim: The stacking between helices α2 and α3 in domain 1 of RF1 is partly disrupted in the RC-RF1•RF3 map.
source: The stacking between helices α2 and α3 in domain 1 of RF1 is partly disrupted and helix α2 has undergone a rotation by 72° away from L11 (Figure 4C,D and E).
evidence: Stated in the results section and supported by Figure 4C,D and E.

claim: Helix α2 has undergone a rotation by 72° away from L11 in the RC-RF1•RF3 map.
source: The stacking between helices α2 and α3 in domain 1 of RF1 is partly disrupted and helix α2 has undergone a rotation by 72° away from L11 (Figure 4C,D and E).
evidence: Stated in the results section and supported by Figure 4C,D and E.

claim: Helix α2 is positioned within binding distance of domain 3 of RF3 in the RC-RF1•RF3 map.
source: Thereby, α2 is positioned within binding distance of domain 3 of RF3 (Figure 4B,C and E) while the contact between the tip of α3 and the P-rich 310-helix in L11 is maintained (Figure 4E) (Petry et al., 2005; Laurberg et al., 2008).
evidence: Stated in the results section with citation support (Petry et al., 2005; Laurberg et al., 2008) and supported by Figure 4B,C and E.

claim: The contact between the tip of α3 and the P-rich 310-helix in L11 is maintained in the RC-RF1•RF3 map.
source: Thereby, α2 is positioned within binding distance of domain 3 of RF3 (Figure 4B,C and E) while the contact between the tip of α3 and the P-rich 310-helix in L11 is maintained (Figure 4E) (Petry et al., 2005; Laurberg et al., 2008).
evidence: Stated in the results section with citation support (Petry et al., 2005; Laurberg et al., 2008) and supported by Figure 4E.

claim: Apo-RF3 in the RC-RF1•RF3 map is observed in a semi-open conformation characterized by a 36° rotation of its domain 3 away from its domain 1.
source: Apo-RF3 in the RC-RF1•RF3 map is observed in a semi-open conformation characterized by a 36° rotation of its domain 3 away from its domain 1 (Figure 5B,D).
evidence: Stated in the results section and supported by Figure 5B,D.

claim: RF3•GTP in the later stage RC-RF3 map is observed in its open conformation with domain 3 rotated 49° away from domain 1 when compared to the closed conformation of free RF3•GDP.
source: RF3•GTP in the later stage RC-RF3 map is observed in its open conformation with domain 3 rotated 49° away from domain 1 when compared to the closed conformation of free RF3•GDP (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: Stated in the results section and supported by Figure 5C,D.

claim: In the semi-open conformation, amino acid stretches R399-Q411 and N458-N467 of RF3 form a cluster of 12 charged or polar amino acids in two flexible loops of domain 3 at the interface with RF1.
source: In the semi-open conformation, amino acid stretches R399-Q411 and N458-N467 of RF3 form a cluster of 12 charged or polar amino acids in two flexible loops of domain 3 at the interface with RF1 (Figure 5E).
evidence: Stated in the results section and supported by Figure 5E.

claim: Helix α2 of RF1 has 5 charged amino acids (H13, E14, E17, E18 and Q20) accessible to interaction with RF3.
source: Examining the surface chemistry of helix α2 of RF1 in the region of interaction with RF3, we find 5 charged amino acids (H13, E14, E17, E18 and Q20), which are accessible to interaction with RF3 (Figure 5F).
evidence: Stated in the results section and supported by Figure 5F.

claim: The surface patch of helix α2 in domain 1 of RF1 that contacts RF3 is negatively charged.
source: The surface patch of helix α2 in domain 1 of RF1 that contacts RF3 is negatively charged (Figure 6A,B), whereas the complementary surface patch in RF3 is positively charged (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: Stated in the results section and supported by Figure 6A,B.

claim: The complementary surface patch in RF3 that contacts RF1 is positively charged.
source: The surface patch of helix α2 in domain 1 of RF1 that contacts RF3 is negatively charged (Figure 6A,B), whereas the complementary surface patch in RF3 is positively charged (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: Stated in the results section and supported by Figure 6C,D.

claim: Amino acid stretches R399-Q411 and N457-N467 of apo-RF3 are involved in a charge-based interaction with helix α2 of RF1 and residues Q74, E75 and H76 of protein S12.
source: The combined observations from fitting (Figure 5D,E) and surface electrostatics (Figure 6A–D) suggest that amino acid stretches R399-Q411 and N457-N467 of apo-RF3 are involved in a charge-based interaction with helix α2 of RF1 and residues Q74, E75 and H76 of protein S12 (Figure 5D).
evidence: Stated in the results section as an inference from fitting and surface electrostatics, supported by Figure 5D,E and Figure 6A–D.

claim: Binding of apo-RF3 to the ribosomal release complex is obtained by formation of a bridge connecting L11-NTD through domain 1 of RF1 with domain 3 of RF3.
source: Thus, binding of apo-RF3 to the ribosomal release complex is obtained by formation of a bridge connecting L11-NTD through domain 1 of RF1 with domain 3 of RF3 (Figures 2E and 4E).
evidence: Stated in the results section as a conclusion from the structural observations, supported by Figures 2E and 4E.

claim: In X-ray structures available for class-1 RFs from RF3-containing Bacteria (E. coli and S. mutans), the surface of helix α2 has an overall electronegative surface potential.
source: Indeed, we find that in X-ray structures available for class-1 RFs from RF3-containing Bacteria (E. coli and S. mutans; Figure 6E), the surface of helix α2 has an overall electronegative surface potential.
evidence: Stated in the results section and supported by Figure 6E.

claim: RF3 from D. vulgaris displays a similar positive surface potential in the same position as observed for RF3 from E. coli.
source: In addition, examining the surface potential in RF3 from D. vulgaris (Figure 6G) (Kihira et al., 2012) we find a similar positive surface potential in the same position as we observed for RF3 from E. coli.
evidence: Stated in the results section with citation support (Kihira et al., 2012) and supported by Figure 6G.

claim: For Bacteria and Archaea lacking RF3 (T. thermophilus and T. maritima), the surface potential of helix α2 is overall electroneutral.
source: In contrast, for Bacteria and Archaea lacking RF3 (T. thermophilus and T. maritima; Figure 6F) the surface potential of helix α2 is overall electroneutral.
evidence: Stated in the results section and supported by Figure 6F.

claim: Charge-based interactions exist between RF1 and apo-RF3.
source: These observations suggest the existence of charge-based interactions between RF1 and apo-RF3.
evidence: Stated in the results section as an inference from the surface potential observations.

claim: RF3 increased the recycling rate of wild-type RF1 by a factor of ten in a GTP-dependent manner.
source: Consistent with earlier reports (Freistroffer et al., 1997; Zavialov et al., 2001; Gao et al., 2007), RF3 increased the recycling rate of wild-type RF1 by a factor of ten in a GTP-dependent manner (Figure 7).
evidence: Stated in the results section with citation support (Freistroffer et al., 1997; Zavialov et al., 2001; Gao et al., 2007) and supported by Figure 7.

claim: The ability of RF3 to recycle wild-type RF1 and RF1 mutants E14A, E17A, and Q20A was similar.
source: The ability of RF3 to recycle wild-type RF1 and RF1 mutants E14A, E17A, and Q20A was similar.
evidence: Stated in the results section describing the mutation analysis.

claim: Recycling of the E18A mutant was reduced threefold compared with recycling of wild-type RF1.
source: In contrast, compared with recycling of wild-type RF1, recycling of the E18A mutant was reduced threefold and recycling of the H13A mutant was reduced 1.4-fold.
evidence: Stated in the results section describing the mutation analysis.

claim: Recycling of the H13A mutant was reduced 1.4-fold compared with recycling of wild-type RF1.
source: In contrast, compared with recycling of wild-type RF1, recycling of the E18A mutant was reduced threefold and recycling of the H13A mutant was reduced 1.4-fold.
evidence: Stated in the results section describing the mutation analysis.

claim: RF3-independent recycling rates of all RF1 variants were indistinguishable.
source: At the same time, RF3-independent recycling rates of all RF1 variants were indistinguishable, showing that the lower recycling of the E18A and H13A mutants was indeed RF3-mediated.
evidence: Stated in the results section describing the mutation analysis.

claim: E18 in the α2-region of RF1 is involved in establishing the negatively charged surface patch important for interaction with the positively charged counterpart in RF3.
source: In light of the findings of surface charge conservation and from the mutation studies, we propose a model in which E18 in the α2-region of RF1 is not only involved in establishing the negatively charged surface patch important for interaction with the positively charged counterpart in RF3 but also involved in a specific interaction with RF3.
evidence: Stated in the results section as a proposed model based on mutation studies and surface charge conservation.

claim: E18 in the α2-region of RF1 is involved in a specific interaction with RF3.
source: In light of the findings of surface charge conservation and from the mutation studies, we propose a model in which E18 in the α2-region of RF1 is not only involved in establishing the negatively charged surface patch important for interaction with the positively charged counterpart in RF3 but also involved in a specific interaction with RF3.
evidence: Stated in the results section as a proposed model based on mutation studies and surface charge conservation.

claim: H13 contributes to optimal orientation of helix α2 including E18 and other residues important for interaction with RF3.
source: We attribute the reduction in RF1 recycling rate by the H13A mutation to indirect—steric and/or charge—effects and propose that H13 contributes to optimal orientation of helix α2 including E18 and other residues important for interaction with RF3.
evidence: Stated in the results section as a proposed model based on mutation studies.

claim: In the X-ray structure of RF3•GDP, the β-phosphate group of GDP is stabilized by interaction with the conserved H92 of RF3.
source: in the X-ray structure of RF3•GDP, the β-phosphate group of GDP is stabilized by interaction with the conserved H92 of RF3 (Figure 8B,E); surprisingly, no Mg2+ ion is participating in this stabilization (Gao et al., 2007).
evidence: Stated in the results section with citation support (Gao et al., 2007) and supported by Figure 8B,E.

claim: No Mg2+ ion participates in stabilization of GDP in the RF3•GDP crystal structure.
source: in the X-ray structure of RF3•GDP, the β-phosphate group of GDP is stabilized by interaction with the conserved H92 of RF3 (Figure 8B,E); surprisingly, no Mg2+ ion is participating in this stabilization (Gao et al., 2007).
evidence: Stated in the results section with citation support (Gao et al., 2007) and supported by Figure 8B,E.

claim: H92 is part of switch region 2.
source: H92 is part of switch region 2; switch regions 1 and 2 are known to be flexible regions involved in activation and deactivation of GTPase activity in RF3.
evidence: Stated in the results section.

claim: Switch regions 1 and 2 are flexible regions involved in activation and deactivation of GTPase activity in RF3.
source: H92 is part of switch region 2; switch regions 1 and 2 are known to be flexible regions involved in activation and deactivation of GTPase activity in RF3.
evidence: Stated in the results section.

claim: Switch region 1 is disordered in the RF3•GDP crystal structure and therefore not resolved.
source: We note that switch region 1 is disordered in the RF3•GDP crystal structure and therefore not resolved.
evidence: Stated in the results section.

claim: In semi-open apo-RF3, H92 is retracted from the nucleotide-binding pocket of RF3.
source: Looking at the position of H92 in semi-open apo-RF3, we observe H92 retracted from the nucleotide-binding pocket of RF3 (Figure 8C,E).
evidence: Stated in the results section and supported by Figure 8C,E.

claim: In the retracted position in semi-open RF3, H92 is unlikely to participate in nucleotide stabilization.
source: In this retracted position—semi-open RF3—H92 is unlikely to participate in nucleotide stabilization.
evidence: Stated in the results section as an inference from the structural observation.

claim: In the open RF3•GTP, H92 is observed in a retracted position where it is not participating in stabilization of GTP.
source: In the later-stage, open RF3•GTP, H92 is observed in a similarly retracted position where it is not participating in stabilization of GTP (Figure 8D,E).
evidence: Stated in the results section and supported by Figure 8D,E.

claim: Coordination of the β-γ phosphates of GTP is performed by a Mg2+ ion in open RF3•GTP.
source: Moreover, coordination of the β-γ phosphates of GTP is performed by a Mg2+ ion, the binding of which is made possible by a well-ordered switch region 1.
evidence: Stated in the results section.

claim: The Mg2+ ion is likely to be essential for GTPase activity.
source: The Mg2+ ion is likely to be essential for GTPase activity (Zhou et al., 2012).
evidence: Stated in the results section with citation support (Zhou et al., 2012).

claim: The release of GDP from RF3 as it changes conformation from closed (RF3•GDP) to semi-open (apo-RF3) is likely triggered by the retraction of H92 from the nucleotide-binding pocket.
source: Hence, the release of GDP from RF3 as it changes conformation from closed (RF3•GDP) to semi-open (apo-RF3) is likely triggered by the retraction of H92 from the nucleotide-binding pocket.
evidence: Stated in the results section as an inference from the structural observations.

claim: The sole interaction between RF3 and L12 involves helix α7 in the G' subdomain of RF3 and helices α4 and α5 in L12-CTD.
source: Based on our fitting, the sole interaction between RF3 and L12 involves helix α7 in the G' subdomain of RF3 and helices α4 and α5 in L12-CTD (Helgstrand et al., 2007), while L12-CTD is clearly separated from L11-NTD by a 14-Å gap (Figure 9A,B and Figure 3A).
evidence: Stated in the results section with citation support (Helgstrand et al., 2007) and supported by Figure 9A,B and Figure 3A.

claim: L12-CTD is clearly separated from L11-NTD by a 14-Å gap in the RC-RF1•RF3 complex.
source: Based on our fitting, the sole interaction between RF3 and L12 involves helix α7 in the G' subdomain of RF3 and helices α4 and α5 in L12-CTD (Helgstrand et al., 2007), while L12-CTD is clearly separated from L11-NTD by a 14-Å gap (Figure 9A,B and Figure 3A).
evidence: Stated in the results section and supported by Figure 9A,B and Figure 3A.

claim: In the RC-RF3•GDPNP map, L12-CTD is observed in contact with both L11-NTD and RF3.
source: In contrast, in the map of the later-stage RC-RF3•GDPNP (Figure 9C,D and Figure 3B) L12-CTD is observed in contact with both L11-NTD and RF3.
evidence: Stated in the results section and supported by Figure 9C,D and Figure 3B.

claim: L12-CTD and RF3 interact prior to formation of a structural bridge with L11-NTD.
source: This suggests that L12-CTD and RF3 interact prior to formation of a structural bridge with L11-NTD.
evidence: Stated in the results section as an inference from the structural observations.

claim: For RF3 to change from apo-RF3 to RF3•GTP, domain 3 must rotate from 36 to 49° away from domain 1.
source: For RF3 to change from apo-RF3 to RF3•GTP, as observed in the RC-RF3•GDPNP complex, domain 3 must rotate even further away from domain 1 (i.e., from 36 to 49°), bringing RF3•GDPNP into its fully open conformation (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: Stated in the results section and supported by Figure 5B–D.

claim: The change from RC-RF1•RF3 to RC-RF3•GDPNP is characterized by a concomitant upward rotation of L12-CTD by ∼45° toward the tip of L11-NTD.
source: Our fitting predicts that the change from RC-RF1•RF3 to RC-RF3•GDPNP is characterized by a concomitant upward rotation of L12-CTD by ∼45° toward the tip of L11-NTD (Figure 9E).
evidence: Stated in the results section as a prediction from fitting and supported by Figure 9E.

claim: The rotation of L12-CTD is accompanied by a 'hinging-in' movement of helices α4 and α5, whereby α4 rotates inward by ∼29° and α5 by ∼11°.
source: This rotation is accompanied by a 'hinging-in' movement of helices α4 and α5, whereby α4 rotates inward by ∼29° and α5 by ∼11° (Figure 9F), leading to formation of a structural bridge between domain 1 of RF3 and a loop in L11-NTD (Figure 9C,D).
evidence: Stated in the results section and supported by Figure 9F.

claim: Similar flexibility in the α4/α5 region of L12 has been observed in earlier studies.
source: Similar flexibility in the α4/α5 region of L12 has been observed in earlier studies (Leijonmarck and Liljas, 1987; Harms et al., 2008; Gao et al., 2009).
evidence: Stated in the results section with citation support (Leijonmarck and Liljas, 1987; Harms et al., 2008; Gao et al., 2009).

claim: L11 undergoes an upward rotation of ∼7° during the change from RC-RF1•RF3 to RC-RF3•GDPNP.
source: Along with the change in position and conformation of L12-CTD observed in the RC-RF1•RF3 and RC-RF3•GDPNP complexes, L11 undergoes an upward rotation of ∼7°, thereby disrupting its interaction with helix α3 in domain 1 of RF1 (Figure 9B,D) and positioning the tip of the L11-NTD for binding to L12-CTD (Figure 9D).
evidence: Stated in the results section and supported by Figure 9B,D.

claim: The upward rotation of L11 disrupts its interaction with helix α3 in domain 1 of RF1.
source: Along with the change in position and conformation of L12-CTD observed in the RC-RF1•RF3 and RC-RF3•GDPNP complexes, L11 undergoes an upward rotation of ∼7°, thereby disrupting its interaction with helix α3 in domain 1 of RF1 (Figure 9B,D) and positioning the tip of the L11-NTD for binding to L12-CTD (Figure 9D).
evidence: Stated in the results section and supported by Figure 9B,D.

claim: The ribosome conformation changes from MS-I to MS-II primarily by intersubunit rotation during the transition from RC-RF1•RF3 to RC-RF3•GDPNP.
source: Furthermore, the ribosome conformation changes—primarily by intersubunit rotation—from MS-I to MS-II, and domain 1 of RF3 moves closer, by a 12° rotation of helix α7, to L6/SRL to form an interaction (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) (Klaholz et al., 2004; Gao et al., 2007; Jin et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2012)
evidence: Stated in the results section with citation support (Klaholz et al., 2004; Gao et al., 2007; Jin et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2012) and supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Domain 1 of RF3 moves closer to L6/SRL by a 12° rotation of helix α7 to form an interaction during the transition from RC-RF1•RF3 to RC-RF3•GDPNP.
source: Furthermore, the ribosome conformation changes—primarily by intersubunit rotation—from MS-I to MS-II, and domain 1 of RF3 moves closer, by a 12° rotation of helix α7, to L6/SRL to form an interaction (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) (Klaholz et al., 2004; Gao et al., 2007; Jin et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2012)
evidence: Stated in the results section with citation support (Klaholz et al., 2004; Gao et al., 2007; Jin et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2012) and supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The region in RF3 occupied by helix α7 constitutes a negatively charged surface patch.
source: It is evident, that the region in RF3 occupied by helix α7 constitutes a negatively charged surface patch (Figure 10A,B), whereas the complementary surface occupied by helices α4 and α5 in L12-CTD is positively charged (Figure 10C,D).
evidence: Stated in the results section and supported by Figure 10A,B.

claim: The complementary surface occupied by helices α4 and α5 in L12-CTD is positively charged.
source: It is evident, that the region in RF3 occupied by helix α7 constitutes a negatively charged surface patch (Figure 10A,B), whereas the complementary surface occupied by helices α4 and α5 in L12-CTD is positively charged (Figure 10C,D).
evidence: Stated in the results section and supported by Figure 10C,D.

claim: IF2, EF-Tu and EF-G show similar negatively charged patches in the proposed area of interaction with L12-CTD.
source: Examination of electrostatics for the other major translational GTPases (IF2, EF-Tu and EF-G) in the proposed area of interaction shows similar negatively charged patches for potential interaction with L12-CTD (Figure 10—figure supplement 1A–F).
evidence: Stated in the results section and supported by Figure 10—figure supplement 1A–F.

claim: The RC-RF1•RF3 structure shows the guanine nucleotide-free apo-form of RF3 in a stable RF1-containing ribosome complex.
source: The RC-RF1•RF3 structure observed here shows the guanine nucleotide-free apo-form of RF3 in a stable RF1-containing ribosome complex.
evidence: Stated in the discussion section.

claim: The existence of the RC-RF1•RF3 structure was predicted from biochemical experiments on the action cycle of RF3.
source: The existence of such a structure was predicted from biochemical experiments on the action cycle of RF3 (Zavialov et al., 2001; Sternberg et al., 2009), but direct experimental evidence has been lacking.
evidence: Stated in the discussion section with citation support (Zavialov et al., 2001; Sternberg et al., 2009).

claim: The affinity of GTP to free RF3 is at least three orders of magnitude lower than that of GDP.
source: It has been shown that the affinity of GTP to free RF3 is at least three orders of magnitude lower than that of GDP and that the average time of spontaneous release of GDP from free RF3 is 30 s (Zavialov et al., 2001)
evidence: Stated in the discussion section with citation support (Zavialov et al., 2001).

claim: The average time of spontaneous release of GDP from free RF3 is 30 s.
source: It has been shown that the affinity of GTP to free RF3 is at least three orders of magnitude lower than that of GDP and that the average time of spontaneous release of GDP from free RF3 is 30 s (Zavialov et al., 2001)
evidence: Stated in the discussion section with citation support (Zavialov et al., 2001).

claim: The release time of GDP from RF3 is comparable with the 100 s of GDP from EF-Tu in the absence of EF-Ts.
source: a release time that is comparable with the 100 s of GDP from EF-Tu in the absence of EF-Ts (Ruusala et al., 1982).
evidence: Stated in the discussion section with citation support (Ruusala et al., 1982).

claim: RF3 exists predominantly in the GDP form in the living cell.
source: The high affinity of GDP to free RF3, possibly due to multiple contacts between H92 of RF3 and the β-phosphate group of GDP (Gao et al., 2007), in combination with the slow dissociation of GDP from RF3 strongly suggests that RF3 exists predominantly in the GDP form in the living cell.
evidence: Stated in the discussion section as an inference from the high affinity of GDP to RF3 and slow dissociation rate, with citation support (Gao et al., 2007).

claim: The class-I RF-bound RC is the guanine nucleotide exchange factor for the G-protein RF3.
source: Moreover, it has been shown that the class-I RF-bound RC is the guanine nucleotide exchange factor for the G-protein RF3 (Zavialov et al., 2001)
evidence: Stated in the discussion section with citation support (Zavialov et al., 2001).

claim: The RC–RF1•RF3 complex contains a form of RF3 from which GDP can readily dissociate and to which GTP can readily associate.
source: an observation that suggests that the RC–RF1•RF3 complex contains a form of RF3 from which GDP can readily dissociate and to which GTP can readily associate.
evidence: Stated in the discussion section as an inference from the observation that the class-I RF-bound RC is the guanine nucleotide exchange factor for RF3.

claim: The novel complex visualized provides the structural basis for the ribosome-dependent guanine nucleotide exchange on RF3.
source: That is, the novel complex visualized here is likely to provide the structural basis for the ribosome-dependent guanine nucleotide exchange on RF3.
evidence: Stated in the discussion section as an inference from the structural observations.

claim: It is RF3 in the compact GDP form that enters the class-1 RF-containing post-termination ribosome complex from which the peptide chain has dissociated after ester bond hydrolysis.
source: Accordingly, it is RF3 in the compact GDP form that enters the class-1 RF-containing post-termination ribosome complex from which the peptide chain has dissociated after ester bond hydrolysis.
evidence: Stated in the discussion section as an inference from the structural and biochemical observations.

claim: The semi-open apo-RF3 structure is formed rapidly by its stabilizing contacts with ribosomal protein L12 and a novel form of RF1.
source: We infer that the semi-open apo-RF3 structure we observe is formed rapidly by its stabilizing contacts with ribosomal protein L12 (Figure 9) and a novel form of RF1.
evidence: Stated in the discussion section as an inference from the structural observations, supported by Figure 9.

claim: The novel form of RF1 is formed concomitantly with formation of the apo-form of RF3.
source: The latter, we propose, is formed concomitantly with formation of the apo-form of RF3 (Figure 11 and Video 1).
evidence: Stated in the discussion section as a proposed model, supported by Figure 11 and Video 1.

claim: The novel form of RF1 stabilizes the binding of the apo-form of RF3 by contact between helix α2 in RF1-domain 1 and domain 3 of apo-RF3.
source: This novel form of RF1 stabilizes the binding of the apo-form of RF3 by contact between helix α2 in RF1-domain 1 and domain 3 of apo-RF3 (Figure 4E).
evidence: Stated in the discussion section as a proposed model, supported by Figure 4E.

claim: The rapid conformational change of RF3 and the stabilization of RF3's apo-form make release of GDP and binding of GTP to RF3 a high-probability event.
source: The rapid conformational change of RF3 and the stabilization of RF3's apo-form make release of GDP and binding of GTP to RF3 a high-probability event and dissociation of RF3•GDP a low-probability event after initial binding of RF3•GDP to the class-1 RF-containing RC.
evidence: Stated in the discussion section as an inference from the structural observations.

claim: Dissociation of RF3•GDP is a low-probability event after initial binding of RF3•GDP to the class-1 RF-containing RC.
source: The rapid conformational change of RF3 and the stabilization of RF3's apo-form make release of GDP and binding of GTP to RF3 a high-probability event and dissociation of RF3•GDP a low-probability event after initial binding of RF3•GDP to the class-1 RF-containing RC.
evidence: Stated in the discussion section as an inference from the structural observations.

claim: L12 and RF1 are essential for the efficient recruitment of RF3 to the RC.
source: This implicates L12 and RF1 as essential for the efficient recruitment of RF3 to the RC.
evidence: Stated in the discussion section as an inference from the structural observations.

claim: L12-CTD has been shown capable of interacting with RF3•GDP.
source: L12-CTD has been shown capable of interacting with RF3•GDP (Helgstrand et al., 2007)
evidence: Stated in the discussion section with citation support (Helgstrand et al., 2007).

claim: GTP binding to RF3 induces the open conformation of the factor thereby driving the ribosome into the intersubunit rotated MS-II state.
source: Conditional on the absence of a peptide chain on the P-site bound tRNA, GTP binding to RF3 induces the open conformation of the factor thereby driving the ribosome into the intersubunit rotated MS-II state (Klaholz et al., 2004; Gao et al., 2007; Jin et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2012).
evidence: Stated in the discussion section with citation support (Klaholz et al., 2004; Gao et al., 2007; Jin et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2012).

claim: A movement of L11 away from domain 1 of RF1 and toward L12 accompanies the change in ribosome conformation to MS-II.
source: A movement of L11 away from domain 1 of RF1 and toward L12 accompanies this change in ribosome conformation (Figure 9).
evidence: Stated in the discussion section and supported by Figure 9.

claim: The structural bridge between the P-rich 310-helix in L11, RF1 domain 1 and RF3 domain 3 is broken during the transition to MS-II.
source: In the process, the structural bridge between the P-rich 310-helix in L11, RF1 domain 1 and RF3 domain 3 (Figures 2E and 4E) is broken and replaced by a structural bridge formed between the tip of L11-NTD, L12-CTD and domain 3 of RF3•GTP (Figure 9C,D and Figure 3B)
evidence: Stated in the discussion section and supported by Figures 2E, 4E, 9C,D and Figure 3B.

claim: A structural bridge is formed between the tip of L11-NTD, L12-CTD and domain 3 of RF3•GTP during the transition to MS-II.
source: In the process, the structural bridge between the P-rich 310-helix in L11, RF1 domain 1 and RF3 domain 3 (Figures 2E and 4E) is broken and replaced by a structural bridge formed between the tip of L11-NTD, L12-CTD and domain 3 of RF3•GTP (Figure 9C,D and Figure 3B)
evidence: Stated in the discussion section and supported by Figure 9C,D and Figure 3B.

claim: The structural bridge between L11-NTD, L12-CTD and domain 3 of RF3•GTP stabilizes RF3•GTP binding to the RC in its MS-II conformation.
source: evidently stabilizing RF3•GTP binding to the RC in its MS-II conformation.
evidence: Stated in the discussion section as an inference from the structural observations.

claim: Domain 1 of the class-1 RF is no longer in contact with the ribosome as a result of the movement of L11.
source: As a result of the movement of L11, domain 1 of the class-1 RF is no longer in contact with the ribosome.
evidence: Stated in the discussion section as an inference from the structural observations.

claim: The semi-open conformation of RF3 has low affinity to both GDP and GTP in analogy with the low affinity of both GDP and GTP to the EF–Tu•Ts complex.
source: Thermodynamically, this scenario requires a much lower affinity of GTP to the semi-open than to the open RF3 conformation (Hauryliuk et al., 2008), implying that the semi-open conformation of RF3 has low affinity to both GDP and GTP in analogy with the low affinity of both GDP and GTP to the EF–Tu•Ts complex (Ruusala et al., 1982).
evidence: Stated in the discussion section as an inference with citation support (Hauryliuk et al., 2008; Ruusala et al., 1982).

claim: The intersubunit-rotated MSII state leads to a steric clash between the ribosome and the class-1 RF.
source: Finally, the intersubunit-rotated MSII state leads to a steric clash between the ribosome and the class-1 RF, which results in the release of the class-1 RF from the A site.
evidence: Stated in the discussion section as an inference from the structural observations.

claim: The steric clash between the ribosome and the class-1 RF results in the release of the class-1 RF from the A site.
source: Finally, the intersubunit-rotated MSII state leads to a steric clash between the ribosome and the class-1 RF, which results in the release of the class-1 RF from the A site.
evidence: Stated in the discussion section as an inference from the structural observations.

claim: RF3 is activated for GTP hydrolysis after the class-1 RF is released.
source: RF3 is activated for GTP hydrolysis and rapidly leaves the ribosome in the GDP form.
evidence: Stated in the discussion section.

claim: RF3 rapidly leaves the ribosome in the GDP form after GTP hydrolysis.
source: RF3 is activated for GTP hydrolysis and rapidly leaves the ribosome in the GDP form.
evidence: Stated in the discussion section.
